Terms.ShortDefinition: The repeating cycle of actions players perform most often during play.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The main thing players do again and again because it feels good and moves them forward.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A clear core loop keeps sessions focused and helps teams prioritize features that reinforce the primary experience.
Terms.Example: In a farming game, plant crops, wait, harvest, sell, and upgrade tools.
Terms.CommonMistake: Adding side systems that never feed back into the loop, so the main experience feels diluted.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write your game's core loop as 4 to 6 verbs and remove any step that does not create progress or feedback.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The full cycle of player input, game response, feedback, and state change.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: What the player does, what the game does back, and how the world updates before the next action.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Understanding the loop helps designers tune pacing, rewards, and failure recovery.
Terms.Example: Move, attack, receive damage feedback, earn loot, upgrade gear, repeat.
Terms.CommonMistake: Treating the game loop as only combat while ignoring downtime, recovery, and preparation.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Map one full cycle of your prototype and mark where feedback arrives after each player action.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A polished sample that demonstrates core gameplay across multiple systems at near-final quality.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A small playable section that shows how the full game should look, feel, and work.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Vertical slices align teams around a shared quality bar before scaling production.
Terms.Example: One combat encounter with final animation, audio, UI, and progression rewards.
Terms.CommonMistake: Calling a rough greybox a vertical slice when art, audio, and feel are still placeholders.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define a one-level slice checklist covering gameplay, UI, audio, and reward feedback.

Terms.ShortDefinition: How players unlock new abilities, content, or power over time.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The path that makes players feel stronger, smarter, or more capable as they keep playing.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Strong progression creates motivation and helps structure content delivery.
Terms.Example: Unlock new biomes after defeating bosses and crafting better gear.
Terms.CommonMistake: Front-loading too many unlocks so later hours feel empty.
Terms.PracticePrompt: List ten unlocks and schedule them across the first five hours of play.

Terms.ShortDefinition: How challenge rises across a game to match growing player skill.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The shape of how hard the game gets from start to finish.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A well-shaped curve prevents boredom early and frustration late.
Terms.Example: Introduce one new enemy type per chapter while gradually reducing reaction time windows.
Terms.CommonMistake: Spiking difficulty without teaching the skills needed to overcome the spike.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Playtest one chapter and chart deaths per encounter to reshape the curve.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Exaggerated visual, audio, and haptic feedback that makes actions feel satisfying.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The extra pop, shake, and sound that makes hitting a button or landing a jump feel great.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Juice improves game feel and helps players understand cause and effect without extra UI.
Terms.Example: Screen shake, particle bursts, and a punchy sound when the player collects a coin.
Terms.CommonMistake: Adding effects everywhere until critical feedback becomes hard to read.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Pick one player action and layer three feedback channels: visual, audio, and motion.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The guided early experience that teaches core mechanics and motivates continued play.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How the game introduces itself and teaches players what to do in the first minutes.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Strong onboarding improves day-one retention and reduces early drop-off.
Terms.Example: A tutorial level that teaches movement, combat, and inventory without long text blocks.
Terms.CommonMistake: Dumping every system into the first ten minutes instead of teaching one skill at a time.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Rewrite your first five minutes so each new input is practiced before the next is introduced.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Long-term goals and systems that sit above individual match or session play.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The bigger goals that keep players coming back after one round ends.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A clear metagame turns short sessions into an ongoing habit.
Terms.Example: Season ranks, collection goals, and weekly challenges that span many matches.
Terms.CommonMistake: Building a metagame before the session loop itself is fun.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define one session goal and one week-long metagame goal that reinforce each other.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A design pattern where greater potential payoff requires accepting greater danger or cost.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Players can play it safe for less, or take a bigger chance for a better payoff.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Risk-reward choices create tension, skill expression, and memorable decisions.
Terms.Example: Entering a high-level dungeon for rare loot while carrying a fragile inventory.
Terms.CommonMistake: Making the risky option strictly worse so players never choose it.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Design three paths through one encounter with different risk and reward profiles.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The player's ability to make meaningful choices that change outcomes.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Feeling like your decisions actually matter in the game world.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Agency creates ownership, replay value, and emotional investment.
Terms.Example: Choosing dialogue that permanently alters which ally joins a late-game mission.
Terms.CommonMistake: Offering cosmetic choices that look meaningful but never affect gameplay or story.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Audit one quest and mark which decisions change systems, narrative, or neither.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The tactile quality of controls, responsiveness, and physical feedback during play.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How good the game feels in your hands when you move, jump, or shoot.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Excellent game feel can make simple mechanics compelling for long sessions.
Terms.Example: A platformer jump with coyote time, jump buffering, and soft landing squash.
Terms.CommonMistake: Blaming content boredom when the real issue is sluggish or imprecise controls.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Record input-to-response delay for jump and attack, then reduce both below 100 ms.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Tuning numbers and rules so options remain viable without a single dominant strategy.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Adjusting systems so no weapon, character, or tactic wins every time.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Balance protects fairness, variety, and long-term engagement.
Terms.Example: Nerfing an overused rifle while buffing underplayed shotguns after telemetry review.
Terms.CommonMistake: Balancing based only on top-player complaints without looking at overall usage data.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Pick three competing options and chart win rate and pick rate after twenty playtests.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The structure of currencies, sources, sinks, and exchanges that shape player progression.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How money, resources, and rewards enter and leave the game.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A healthy economy supports pacing, monetization, and long-term goals without inflation.
Terms.Example: Gold earned from quests and spent on upgrades, repairs, and cosmetics.
Terms.CommonMistake: Adding infinite earn rates without sinks, so prices and progression break.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Draw a source-and-sink diagram for one currency and verify every source has a matching sink.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Crafting spaces, encounters, and routes that teach, challenge, and reward players.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Building the places where gameplay actually happens.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Level design translates systems into memorable experiences and readable challenge.
Terms.Example: A stealth level with safe paths, risky shortcuts, and a scripted discovery moment.
Terms.CommonMistake: Decorating a map before verifying traversal, sightlines, and encounter flow.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Greybox one room that teaches a new mechanic using layout alone, with no tutorial text.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A system where an action's result encourages or discourages repeating that action.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: When doing something makes the next attempt easier, harder, or more tempting.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Feedback loops drive mastery, addiction risk, and strategic depth.
Terms.Example: Landing combos fills a meter that unlocks stronger finishers.
Terms.CommonMistake: Creating runaway positive loops with no counterplay or soft caps.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Identify one positive and one negative feedback loop in your prototype and document their caps.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A technique where reusable objects are created in advance and activated when needed instead of repeatedly creating and destroying them.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Keep a collection of reusable objects instead of constantly creating new ones.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Pooling reduces allocation spikes and garbage collection pressure during intense gameplay.
Terms.Example: Reuse bullet instances by disabling them after impact and returning them to a pool.
Terms.CommonMistake: Growing pools forever without a max size, eventually wasting more memory than spawning.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Implement a bullet pool with Get and Release methods and compare GC spikes before and after.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Automatic memory cleanup that reclaims unused objects during runtime.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The system that finds memory you are no longer using and frees it for you.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Collection pauses can cause frame hitches, especially on mobile and console targets.
Terms.Example: Allocating new strings every frame can trigger frequent GC spikes.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ignoring allocation hotspots and only blaming the GC itself.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Profile one gameplay scene and list the top three allocation sources in Update.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A model where an object exists in one state at a time and transitions based on rules.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A system that switches behavior cleanly between modes like idle, run, jump, or attack.
Terms.WhyItMatters: State machines make complex character and AI behavior easier to debug and extend.
Terms.Example: An enemy transitions from patrol to chase when the player enters detection range.
Terms.CommonMistake: Allowing multiple conflicting states to be active with no clear ownership.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Draw a four-state player controller and define every legal transition.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Converting runtime data into a storable or transmittable format and back again.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Turning game data into save files, network packets, or config files.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Reliable serialization is essential for saves, multiplayer sync, and content pipelines.
Terms.Example: Write player inventory to JSON before closing the app.
Terms.CommonMistake: Changing save formats without migration, which silently breaks older player files.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Save and load one inventory object, then add a version field and a migration path.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A pattern where required services are provided to a class instead of created inside it.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Pass in the tools a class needs rather than building them internally.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Injection improves testability and reduces tight coupling between systems.
Terms.Example: Inject an audio service into a weapon class instead of calling a global singleton.
Terms.CommonMistake: Hiding new dependencies behind static singletons that make tests brittle.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Refactor one gameplay class to receive its dependencies through the constructor.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Updating simulation logic at a constant interval independent of frame rate.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Run physics and gameplay logic on a steady clock so results stay consistent.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Fixed timesteps keep physics stable and make networked games easier to synchronize.
Terms.Example: Run physics at 50 Hz while rendering as fast as the GPU allows.
Terms.CommonMistake: Mixing render-frame movement with physics forces without interpolation.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Move a rigidbody with fixed delta time and compare behavior at 30 FPS and 60 FPS.

Terms.ShortDefinition: An architecture where gameplay data lives in components and behavior runs in systems over entities.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Store traits in small data chunks and let systems process matching groups efficiently.
Terms.WhyItMatters: ECS can improve performance and scale for large numbers of similar game objects.
Terms.Example: A movement system updates every entity that has position and velocity components.
Terms.CommonMistake: Stuffing unrelated data into one giant component and losing the data-oriented benefit.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Model a projectile as separate transform, velocity, and lifetime components.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The elapsed time since the previous frame, used to keep motion frame-rate independent.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How long the last frame took, so movement stays smooth on fast and slow devices.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Using delta time prevents gameplay speed from changing with frame rate.
Terms.Example: position += velocity * deltaTime;
Terms.CommonMistake: Multiplying forces by delta time twice, or forgetting it in one code path.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Move an object with and without delta time at unlocked frame rates and compare distance traveled.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A messaging pattern where systems publish events and listeners react without direct references.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: One part of the game announces something happened, and other parts can listen and respond.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Events reduce tight coupling and help UI, audio, and gameplay stay in sync.
Terms.Example: A HealthChanged event updates the HUD and plays a hurt sound.
Terms.CommonMistake: Creating anonymous listeners that are never unsubscribed, causing leaks and double callbacks.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add a PlayerDied event with one gameplay listener and one UI listener.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Encapsulating actions as objects so they can be queued, undone, replayed, or networked.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Turn each player action into a little package that can be stored and replayed.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Commands support undo, replays, AI scripting, and deterministic multiplayer inputs.
Terms.Example: Store move and attack commands for a turn-based match and replay them later.
Terms.CommonMistake: Mutating game state outside the command, so undo cannot restore the previous state.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create UndoableCommand for placing and removing a building tile.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The per-frame engine cycle that processes input, simulation, and presentation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The heartbeat of the game that runs every frame.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Knowing what belongs in update versus fixed update prevents timing bugs.
Terms.Example: Read input in Update, simulate physics in FixedUpdate, and follow cameras in LateUpdate.
Terms.CommonMistake: Doing expensive work every frame that could run on a timer or event.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Move one system out of Update into an event or coroutine and measure CPU savings.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A function that can pause and resume over multiple frames without blocking the main thread.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A script that waits and continues later while the game keeps running.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Coroutines simplify timed sequences, fades, and async gameplay flows on one thread.
Terms.Example: Fade out a UI panel over one second using yield return null each frame.
Terms.CommonMistake: Starting many long-lived coroutines without cancellation when the object is disabled.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write a damage-over-time coroutine that stops cleanly when the target dies.

Terms.ShortDefinition: An approach that organizes data for cache-friendly processing instead of around objects first.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Arrange data so the CPU can process lots of similar values quickly.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Data-oriented design unlocks performance for large simulations and ECS architectures.
Terms.Example: Store all enemy health values in one array processed by a single system.
Terms.CommonMistake: Keeping object-oriented wrappers that defeat contiguous data layout.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Rewrite one particle update to iterate arrays of positions and velocities.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A Unity data asset that stores shared configuration outside scene objects.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A reusable settings file that lives in the project instead of on every prefab.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Scriptable objects make balancing and content iteration safer and faster.
Terms.Example: A WeaponStats asset shared by every rifle prefab instance.
Terms.CommonMistake: Storing mutable runtime state in assets that accidentally persist between play sessions.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create a ScriptableObject for enemy stats and assign it to three enemy prefabs.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Measuring where CPU, GPU, memory, and time are spent to guide optimization.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Using tools to find what is actually slow instead of guessing.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Profiling prevents wasted optimization effort and protects frame budgets.
Terms.Example: Capture a deep profile during combat and sort functions by self time.
Terms.CommonMistake: Optimizing code that never appears in the profile hotspots.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Capture one play session profile and list three actionable hotspots with owners.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A command that tells the GPU to render a batch of geometry with a specific material setup.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Each request sent to the GPU to draw something on screen.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Too many draw calls can bottleneck rendering, especially on mobile GPUs.
Terms.Example: Ten unique materials on ten objects may produce ten separate draw calls.
Terms.CommonMistake: Breaking batches with unique materials when a shared atlas would suffice.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Count draw calls in a scene, then atlas two materials and measure the reduction.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A rendering optimization that skips objects hidden behind other geometry.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Do not render things the player cannot see.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Rendering invisible objects wastes GPU resources.
Terms.Example: Rooms behind a closed door are excluded from the render list.
Terms.CommonMistake: Expecting occlusion culling to fix overdraw from transparent VFX.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Bake occlusion data for one interior level and compare GPU timings with it disabled.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Skipping objects outside the camera view volume before rendering.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Ignore objects that are off-screen or behind the camera.
Terms.WhyItMatters: It avoids wasting GPU work on geometry the player will never see in the current frame.
Terms.Example: Trees behind the camera are removed from the render queue.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using giant bounding volumes that keep off-screen props in the frustum.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Visualize camera frustum bounds and tighten one oversized collider.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Using simpler versions of assets at greater distances to save rendering cost.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Show a detailed model up close and a cheaper one far away.
Terms.WhyItMatters: LOD preserves visual quality near the player while protecting frame rate.
Terms.Example: A hero mesh swaps to a lower polygon version beyond 30 meters.
Terms.CommonMistake: Switching LODs so abruptly that popping is obvious to players.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create three LOD meshes for one prop and tune transition distances in play mode.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Rendering the same screen pixel multiple times due to overlapping transparent or layered geometry.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Drawing on top of the same pixel again and again.
Terms.WhyItMatters: High overdraw can crush fill-rate performance, especially on mobile GPUs.
Terms.Example: Multiple fullscreen particle layers stacking in the same view.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using huge transparent quads when smaller clipped meshes would suffice.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Enable an overdraw debug view and reduce the worst particle effect by half.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A shading approach that mimics how light interacts with real-world materials.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Materials react to light in a realistic, consistent way across different scenes.
Terms.WhyItMatters: PBR helps art look cohesive under varied lighting and reduces guesswork for artists.
Terms.Example: Metal reflects sharply while rough wood scatters light softly using the same shader model.
Terms.CommonMistake: Mixing PBR maps with non-PBR lighting assumptions, creating plastic-looking materials.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Author one material with albedo, roughness, and metallic maps under two lighting setups.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A GPU program that calculates how surfaces are drawn, shaded, and transformed.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The little program that tells the GPU how each pixel or vertex should look.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Shaders define visual style and often dominate GPU cost.
Terms.Example: A toon shader that remaps lighting into hard bands for a comic look.
Terms.CommonMistake: Writing complex fragment logic when a cheaper material feature would work.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create a simple unlit color shader and apply it to a test mesh.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The ordered stages and systems that take scene data and produce the final image.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The factory line that turns game objects into pixels on screen.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Pipeline choice affects quality features, platform support, and performance characteristics.
Terms.Example: Using a lightweight forward pipeline for mobile and a deferred pipeline for consoles.
Terms.CommonMistake: Enabling every pipeline feature without checking target device cost.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare one scene's frame time under two quality pipeline settings.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Combining non-moving meshes that share materials into fewer draw calls.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Group still objects together so the GPU draws them more efficiently.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Static batching is a major win for environment art on constrained devices.
Terms.Example: Hundreds of static crates sharing one material drawn as fewer batches.
Terms.CommonMistake: Marking dynamic objects as static and breaking their movement or lighting.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Enable static batching on a prop group and measure draw-call reduction.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Runtime combining of small moving meshes that share material setup.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Automatically group tiny moving objects to reduce draw requests.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Dynamic batching can help simple scenes, but has strict mesh and material limits.
Terms.Example: Many small debris pieces with identical materials batched each frame.
Terms.CommonMistake: Expecting dynamic batching to save large unique meshes that exceed limits.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create twenty tiny quads and inspect whether they batch in the frame debugger.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A depth buffer that stores per-pixel distance so closer surfaces can occlude farther ones.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A hidden map of how far away each pixel is from the camera.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Depth testing is fundamental to correct sorting of opaque geometry.
Terms.Example: A character standing in front of a wall correctly hides the wall pixels.
Terms.CommonMistake: Fighting transparent sorting issues with z-buffer tricks that create artifacts.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Render two overlapping cubes and inspect the depth buffer visualization.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A technique that renders the scene from a light's view to determine which pixels are shadowed.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The light takes a depth photo, then the camera checks what is hidden from that light.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Shadows add realism but are among the most expensive lighting features.
Terms.Example: Cascaded shadow maps covering near detail and far terrain under sunlight.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using oversized shadow resolutions on mobile without cascade tuning.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Toggle shadows on a key light and measure GPU frame-time impact.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Full-screen image effects applied after the main scene is rendered.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Filters and polish layered on top of the finished picture.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Post effects sell mood and readability, but can dominate GPU fill cost.
Terms.Example: Bloom, color grading, and mild chromatic aberration on a cinematic shot.
Terms.CommonMistake: Stacking multiple expensive effects that barely change the intended look.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Enable only two post effects and A/B the scene for mood versus cost.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A chain of progressively smaller texture versions used when sampling distant surfaces.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Smaller copies of a texture that the GPU uses when things are far away.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Mipmaps reduce aliasing and improve texture sampling performance.
Terms.Example: A brick wall uses a lower mip level when viewed from across a courtyard.
Terms.CommonMistake: Disabling mipmaps on world textures and introducing shimmering aliasing.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Inspect mip visualization on one material and confirm distant surfaces use lower mips.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Rendering with color values beyond the 0-1 display range, then tone-mapping to screen output.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Working with brighter-than-screen light values, then compressing them for the display.
Terms.WhyItMatters: HDR enables bloom, realistic lighting contrast, and better exposure control.
Terms.Example: Sunlit exteriors and dark interiors shared in one scene with exposure adaptation.
Terms.CommonMistake: Enabling HDR without tone mapping, producing clipped or washed-out results.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare one scene in LDR and HDR with identical lighting intensity.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A texture that fakes fine surface detail by altering how light interacts with a mesh.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A flat image that makes a surface look bumpy or detailed without extra geometry.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Normal maps add visual richness while keeping polygon counts practical.
Terms.Example: Brick wall detail is painted into a normal map on a simple plane.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using a normal map authored for the wrong tangent space, causing lighting seams.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Apply a normal map to a flat quad and rotate a light around it to verify detail.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Building the bone and control structure that deforms a character model during animation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Creating the skeleton and handles that make a model move.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A clean rig determines how expressive, stable, and reusable animations can be.
Terms.Example: Shoulder, spine, and finger controls are added to a hero character mesh.
Terms.CommonMistake: Overcomplicating controls so animators fight the rig instead of posing.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Build a simple biped rig with IK legs and test a walk cycle.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Binding mesh vertices to bones so the model follows skeletal animation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Connecting a character mesh to its skeleton so it bends correctly.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Poor skin weights create ugly deformation and break immersion.
Terms.Example: Elbow vertices follow upper and lower arm bones with blended influence.
Terms.CommonMistake: Leaving heavy weight influences across joints that should bend cleanly.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Paint weights on a shoulder and compare deformation before and after cleanup.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Flattening a 3D surface into 2D texture coordinates for painting and shading.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Unwrapping a model so textures can be painted on it like wrapping paper.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Good UV layouts improve texture clarity and reduce visible seams.
Terms.Example: A character torso is unwrapped so armor details align across mesh islands.
Terms.CommonMistake: Stretching UVs unevenly, which makes textures look warped in-game.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Unwrap a crate and check texel density consistency across all faces.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A single image containing multiple frames or icons arranged for efficient rendering.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: One texture file that holds many animation frames or UI icons together.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Sprite sheets reduce draw calls and simplify 2D animation workflows.
Terms.Example: A character walk cycle stored as eight frames in one PNG atlas.
Terms.CommonMistake: Packing frames with no padding, causing neighbor bleed when filtering.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Pack a six-frame attack animation into one sheet and play it in engine.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Defining important poses at points in time and interpolating motion between them.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Set the important poses, then let the computer fill in the in-between movement.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Keyframes are the foundation of most authored character and prop animation.
Terms.Example: A jump keyed at crouch, takeoff, apex, and landing.
Terms.CommonMistake: Keying every frame manually and destroying editable timing.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Animate a door opening with only four keys and adjust easing.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Mixing multiple animation clips to create smooth transitions or combined motion.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Crossfading or combining animations so movement does not pop.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Blending keeps locomotion and combat responsive without hard cuts.
Terms.Example: Blend walk and strafe clips based on analog stick direction.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using long blend times that make controls feel laggy.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Set up a blend tree for idle, walk, and run and tune transition durations.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Calculating joint rotations so an end effector reaches a target position.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Tell the hand or foot where to go, and the limb figures out how to bend.
Terms.WhyItMatters: IK improves grounding, aiming, and interaction with uneven surfaces.
Terms.Example: Feet plant on stairs while the hips adjust automatically.
Terms.CommonMistake: Over-constraining IK so limbs snap into unnatural poses.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add two-bone IK to a character leg and test foot placement on a ramp.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Recording real performer movement and transferring it onto a digital character.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Capture a person's motion with sensors or cameras and apply it to a 3D character.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Mo-cap accelerates realistic animation production for cinematic and gameplay needs.
Terms.Example: A fight choreography recorded on a stage and cleaned for an in-game finisher.
Terms.CommonMistake: Shipping raw capture without cleanup, leaving foot slides and noise.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Plan a short capture shot list with cleanup and retargeting steps.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A morph target that stores vertex offsets to reshape a mesh for expressions or variation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A saved mesh shape you can dial up to smile, frown, or change form.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Blend shapes are essential for faces, damage states, and body variation.
Terms.Example: A character face uses smile, blink, and brow-raise shapes driven by dialogue.
Terms.CommonMistake: Stacking too many high-resolution shapes that blow memory budgets.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create three facial blend shapes and drive them from a simple slider UI.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A base color texture without lighting or specular information baked in.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The flat color of a surface before lighting is applied.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Clean albedo maps are required for believable PBR materials.
Terms.Example: A wood plank albedo shows grain color without fake shadows.
Terms.CommonMistake: Baking ambient occlusion or highlights into albedo and breaking lighting response.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Repaint one material albedo to remove baked shadows and compare under two lights.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A texture controlling how sharp or blurry reflections appear across a surface.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Dark areas look glossier and bright areas look more matte.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Roughness variation sells material realism more than color alone.
Terms.Example: Metal edges stay glossy while worn paint reads rough and chalky.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using gloss and roughness maps interchangeably without converting the workflow.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Paint a roughness map for a metal panel with scratched edges and preview reflections.

Terms.ShortDefinition: How many texture pixels cover a given amount of world-space surface.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How sharp or muddy a texture looks for its real-world size.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Consistent texel density keeps environments readable and fair across assets.
Terms.Example: A door and nearby wall share roughly the same pixels-per-meter.
Terms.CommonMistake: UV-scaling hero props denser than architecture, making walls look blurry by comparison.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Measure texel density on three props and normalize them to one target value.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Transferring animation from one skeleton onto another with different proportions.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Reuse a walk cycle on characters that are not built on the exact same skeleton.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Retargeting multiplies animation value across a cast of characters.
Terms.Example: Apply the same dance clip to a child and adult avatar with mapping adjustments.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ignoring bone naming and proportion differences, which creates foot skating.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Retarget one clip to a second rig and fix foot contact in the result.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A collection of reusable tiles used to construct 2D levels and environments.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A palette of small art pieces you stamp repeatedly to build maps.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Tilesets speed 2D production and keep art style consistent across levels.
Terms.Example: Grass, water, and cliff tiles assemble into a top-down overworld.
Terms.CommonMistake: Designing tiles that only connect in one orientation, limiting level variety.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create a nine-slice terrain tileset and build a small path that uses every tile.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Everyday sound effects recorded to match on-screen physical actions.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Custom recorded sounds for footsteps, cloth, impacts, and object handling.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Foley makes interactions feel tactile and grounded in the game world.
Terms.Example: Recording leather creaks and metal clanks for a character gear swap.
Terms.CommonMistake: Reusing one footstep sample on every surface, which breaks believability.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Record three surface footsteps and hook them to a movement animation.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Sound that exists within the game world and can be heard by characters.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Audio that comes from something in the scene, like a radio or monster roar.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Diegetic audio strengthens world believability and spatial storytelling.
Terms.Example: An alarm siren inside a facility that characters react to.
Terms.CommonMistake: Playing world sounds without distance attenuation, so they feel detached.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Place one diegetic emitter and verify volume falloff as the player walks away.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Temporarily lowering one sound layer so another can be heard clearly.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Turning background audio down when something important needs attention.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Ducking preserves clarity for dialogue, warnings, and critical gameplay cues.
Terms.Example: Music volume dips while a mission briefing voice line plays.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ducking too aggressively so the mix feels like it keeps collapsing.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Set a ducking rule that lowers music 6 dB during dialogue.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Music that changes layers or intensity based on gameplay state.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The soundtrack reacts to combat, exploration, or story moments in real time.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Adaptive music keeps emotional pacing aligned with player actions without jarring loops.
Terms.Example: Combat drums layer in when enemies appear and fade when the fight ends.
Terms.CommonMistake: Hard-cutting between unrelated tracks instead of layered transitions.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Design a two-layer exploration and combat bed with a crossfade trigger.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Positioning sound in 3D space so players can locate sources by ear.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Hearing where a sound is coming from around you.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Spatial audio supports stealth, awareness, and immersion.
Terms.Example: Footsteps approaching from the left warn the player before an enemy appears.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using stereo-only clips for critical directional cues.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Place three emitters around the player and verify left, right, and rear localization.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Balancing buses, levels, and priorities so the soundtrack remains clear under gameplay load.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Organizing and leveling music, dialogue, and effects so nothing fights for attention.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A disciplined mix protects readability during chaotic moments.
Terms.Example: Separate buses for UI, combat SFX, dialogue, and music with priority rules.
Terms.CommonMistake: Leaving every sound at default loudness until the mix becomes unreadable.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Build a four-bus mixer and assign five existing sounds into the correct buses.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The layered ambient audio bed that defines a location's atmosphere.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The background mood of a place made from many quiet sounds.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Soundscapes sell setting before the player sees every prop.
Terms.Example: Wind, distant traffic, and HVAC hum establish a rooftop at night.
Terms.CommonMistake: Looping one short bed that becomes obviously repetitive within seconds.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Create a 30-second location bed using at least three overlapping loops.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Simulated reflections that make sounds feel like they exist in a physical space.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Echo and room tone that tell your ears how big a space is.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Reverb cues environment scale and can support stealth or horror design.
Terms.Example: Footsteps ring longer in a cathedral than in a carpeted hallway.
Terms.CommonMistake: Applying one global reverb to every location, flattening spatial contrast.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Assign different reverb presets to a cave and a closet and A/B walkthroughs.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Specialized tools such as FMOD or Wwise that manage interactive audio outside the game engine.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A dedicated audio engine that designers use to build complex sound behavior.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Middleware lets audio teams iterate without constant engineering changes.
Terms.Example: An FMOD event randomizes footsteps and adapts to surface parameters.
Terms.CommonMistake: Hardcoding complex audio logic in engine code that audio designers cannot edit.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Prototype one interactive event in middleware and trigger it from gameplay.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Combining multiple sound elements into one impactful effect.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Stacking smaller sounds to make one hit, explosion, or UI click feel bigger.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Layering creates richness and control without relying on a single recording.
Terms.Example: A gunshot built from mechanical click, muzzle blast, and distant tail.
Terms.CommonMistake: Layering too many elements so the result becomes muddy and undefined.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Build a three-layer UI confirm sound and balance each layer's contribution.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Recorded spoken performance used for characters, narration, or system prompts.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Actors speaking lines that play in the game.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Voice over carries story, personality, and critical instructions.
Terms.Example: A companion character warns the player about an ambush mid-mission.
Terms.CommonMistake: Shipping dialogue without localization or subtitle fallbacks.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write and record three system VO lines with matching subtitle timing.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Reducing audio file size or dynamic range for memory, bandwidth, or mix control.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making sounds smaller to store or quieter in the loud parts so they sit better in a mix.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Compression keeps mobile packages manageable and mixes controlled.
Terms.Example: Converting long music beds to a compressed format for a mobile build.
Terms.CommonMistake: Over-compressing effects until they lose punch and clarity.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare file size and quality for one clip at two compression settings.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Matching perceived volume across content to platform loudness targets.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making sure no track or trailer is randomly much louder than another.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Normalization prevents player fatigue and meets store or console requirements.
Terms.Example: Dialog and music beds both target the same integrated loudness range.
Terms.CommonMistake: Normalizing peak level only, which still leaves large loudness swings.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Measure integrated loudness for three clips and bring them into the same target range.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Using device vibration or force feedback to reinforce game actions through touch.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making the controller or phone buzz so actions feel physical.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Haptics strengthen game feel and accessibility of important cues.
Terms.Example: A short rumble when the player lands a heavy attack.
Terms.CommonMistake: Firing haptics for every minor event until players turn them off.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Design three haptic patterns for hit, miss, and low health warning.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Sound that exists for the audience and not as a source inside the story world.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Music or narration the characters would not hear.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Non-diegetic layers guide emotion and pacing without needing a world emitter.
Terms.Example: A tense score swells during a chase even though no radio is playing in-world.
Terms.CommonMistake: Mixing non-diegetic score so loudly that gameplay cues become hard to hear.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Mark five sounds in your project as diegetic or non-diegetic and justify each choice.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The delay between sending an action and seeing its result across a network.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How long it takes for your input to reach the game and come back.
Terms.WhyItMatters: High latency makes controls feel sluggish and can break competitive fairness.
Terms.Example: A player fires on an enemy that has already moved on the server.
Terms.CommonMistake: Blaming only ping while ignoring jitter and packet loss.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Log round-trip time during a session and note gameplay moments that feel delayed.

Terms.ShortDefinition: How many times per second the server updates simulation and networking state.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How often the server processes the game world each second.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Higher tick rates can improve precision but increase server and bandwidth cost.
Terms.Example: A shooter server running 60 simulation ticks per second.
Terms.CommonMistake: Raising tick rate without profiling CPU and bandwidth budgets.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare hit registration quality at two tick rates in a controlled test.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Letting the local client simulate actions immediately before server confirmation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Move on your screen right away even though the server has not confirmed yet.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Prediction hides network delay and keeps movement feeling responsive.
Terms.Example: A player jumps locally while waiting for the authoritative server position.
Terms.CommonMistake: Failing to reconcile when the server rejects the predicted state.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Implement predicted movement and log corrections when the server disagrees.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Rewinding and replaying simulation frames when late network inputs arrive.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Undo a few frames and replay them with the correct inputs once they arrive.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Rollback enables responsive fighting and action games over real-world networks.
Terms.Example: A fighting game corrects a hit after the remote input finally reaches the host.
Terms.CommonMistake: Rolling back without deterministic simulation, which creates endless desyncs.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Prototype a tiny deterministic sim and delay one input to observe rollback repair.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A server that owns the true game state and validates player actions.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The server decides what really happened, not each player's device.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Authority prevents cheating and keeps multiplayer outcomes consistent.
Terms.Example: The server confirms a hit before damage is applied, even if a client predicted it locally.
Terms.CommonMistake: Trusting client-reported damage values without server validation.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Move damage resolution to the server and reject an illegal client claim.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Server-side techniques that account for latency when validating hits or interactions.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The server rewinds history a bit so shots still make sense for high-ping players.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Lag compensation improves fairness in shooters without letting clients decide hits.
Terms.Example: A hitscan shot is tested against where the target was when the shooter fired.
Terms.CommonMistake: Rewinding too far, which creates shoot-behind-cover frustration.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Document a rewind window policy and test it at 50 ms and 150 ms latency.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Correcting the local client state when the authoritative server result differs from prediction.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: When the server's truth arrives, smoothly fix your local guess.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Reconciliation keeps prediction responsive without drifting forever from reality.
Terms.Example: A predicted dash is corrected when the server says a wall blocked part of the move.
Terms.CommonMistake: Snapping hard to server state every correction, creating visible rubber-banding.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add reconciliation with interpolation so corrections are less noticeable.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Copying relevant object state from the authority to remote clients.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Keeping other players' characters and objects updated on your machine.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Replication strategy determines bandwidth cost and perceived smoothness.
Terms.Example: Only replicate position, health, and team for distant players.
Terms.CommonMistake: Replicating every variable every tick regardless of relevance.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define a replication set for one enemy type and cut three unnecessary fields.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Smoothing remote entity motion by blending between recently received states.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Fill in the gaps between network updates so remote players look smooth.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Interpolation hides tickiness caused by discrete network snapshots.
Terms.Example: A remote runner is rendered slightly in the past between two pose updates.
Terms.CommonMistake: Interpolating without a buffer, which causes stutter when packets jitter.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Buffer two snapshots and interpolate a remote transform between them.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Network packets that never arrive and must be recovered or tolerated by the game.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Some messages vanish on the way and never show up.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Games must stay playable even when the network drops data.
Terms.Example: A lost input packet is resent or reconstructed from later state.
Terms.CommonMistake: Assuming a perfect network during design and playtesting only on LAN.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Simulate 5 percent packet loss and list which systems break first.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Variation in packet arrival time that makes latency unstable.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Ping that jumps around instead of staying steady.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Jitter causes hitching even when average latency looks acceptable.
Terms.Example: Packets arrive at 40 ms, then 90 ms, then 35 ms in quick succession.
Terms.CommonMistake: Tuning only for average ping and ignoring arrival variance.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Graph packet arrival deltas during a match and compute jitter range.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Systems that group players into sessions based on rules like skill, region, or party size.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Finding fair opponents or teammates automatically.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Matchmaking quality strongly affects retention and perceived fairness.
Terms.Example: Players are matched within a skill rating range and the same region.
Terms.CommonMistake: Expanding search so far that matches become unfair just to reduce queue time.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write matchmaking rules for skill, latency, and max queue time tradeoffs.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Techniques that help peers connect through home routers and network address translation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Helping two phones or PCs find each other even behind routers.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Traversal failures are a common cause of join errors in peer-hosted games.
Terms.Example: STUN or relay fallback lets two mobile players connect successfully.
Terms.CommonMistake: Assuming all players can host without providing a relay option.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Document a connection path: direct, STUN, then TURN relay fallback.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A persistent authoritative host that runs independently of any player's device.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A always-on game server that is not tied to one player's phone or console.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Dedicated servers improve stability, anti-cheat, and session continuity.
Terms.Example: A battle-royale match runs on cloud servers even if the creator disconnects.
Terms.CommonMistake: Using listen servers for competitive modes that need stronger authority.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare cheat risk and disconnect handling for listen versus dedicated hosting.

Terms.ShortDefinition: When simulated game states diverge across machines that should match.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Players or systems no longer agree on what is true in the match.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Desyncs break multiplayer integrity and are hard to debug without determinism.
Terms.Example: One client sees a door closed while another sees it open.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ignoring non-deterministic APIs like unordered iteration or unsafe random calls.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add a checksum of critical state each tick and log the first mismatch.

Terms.ShortDefinition: When a device reduces CPU or GPU performance to prevent overheating.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The phone slows itself down because it is getting too hot.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Throttling can cause sudden frame drops during long play sessions.
Terms.Example: A game holds 60 FPS for ten minutes, then drops after sustained GPU load.
Terms.CommonMistake: Blaming one short frame spike for thermal issues that only appear after long sessions.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Run a 20-minute combat soak on device and chart FPS against skin temperature.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Reducing texture memory footprint using GPU-friendly compressed formats.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Shrink image files so they use less RAM and load faster on device.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Compression is critical for fitting art within mobile memory budgets.
Terms.Example: Authoring albedo maps in ASTC for iOS and ETC2 for Android targets.
Terms.CommonMistake: Shipping uncompressed textures to save artist time while blowing memory budgets.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Convert one atlas to a platform compressed format and compare memory before and after.

Terms.ShortDefinition: When available device memory is low enough that the OS may reclaim app resources.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The device is running low on RAM and may force your app to free memory or close.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Memory pressure causes crashes, reloads, and degraded performance on mobile.
Terms.Example: Background apps are purged and your game reloads textures after a large scene load.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ignoring low-memory warnings until players report unexplained reloads.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Force a heavy scene load on a low-end device and log memory warnings.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Dynamically lowering visual or simulation quality to maintain stable frame rate on device.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The game quietly reduces effects or resolution when the phone starts struggling.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Adaptive performance helps sustain playable frame rates during long or demanding sessions.
Terms.Example: Shadow quality drops after sustained GPU load while keeping gameplay at 30 FPS.
Terms.CommonMistake: Dropping quality so aggressively that the game becomes visually confusing.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define three quality tiers and automatic triggers based on frame time and thermal state.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The screen region guaranteed to be visible and interactive outside notches and system bars.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The part of the phone screen where UI will not be covered by cutouts or home indicators.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Respecting safe areas prevents clipped buttons and unreadable HUD on modern devices.
Terms.Example: Health bars and menus inset to avoid the notch and rounded corners.
Terms.CommonMistake: Hardcoding offsets for one phone model and breaking layouts on others.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Place a pause button using safe-area insets and verify on notch and non-notch layouts.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Gameplay and UI control driven by finger contact, gestures, and multi-touch.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Players tap, swipe, and pinch instead of using a mouse or controller.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Touch design determines accessibility, precision, and comfort on phones.
Terms.Example: A virtual joystick plus swipe-to-dodge mapped to one-handed play.
Terms.CommonMistake: Requiring tiny hit targets that fail fat-finger usability.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Increase one critical button hit area to at least 44 points and retest one-handed play.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Delivering frames at consistent intervals so motion feels smooth even when FPS is capped.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Spacing frames evenly so gameplay does not feel stuttery.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Uneven pacing feels worse than a slightly lower but stable frame rate.
Terms.Example: Locking presentation to 30 FPS with steady intervals instead of oscillating 45 to 25.
Terms.CommonMistake: Chasing peak FPS while ignoring frame-time variance.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Capture frame-time graphs before and after enabling consistent pacing.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Scaling render resolution up or down at runtime to protect frame rate.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Drawing the game a bit blurrier when needed so it stays smooth.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Dynamic resolution is a powerful lever for GPU-bound mobile titles.
Terms.Example: Internal resolution drops during particle-heavy fights, then recovers in quieter scenes.
Terms.CommonMistake: Scaling so far that UI or targeting readability collapses.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Set min and max scale factors and verify readability at the lowest setting.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Reducing CPU, GPU, network, and wake work so play sessions drain less power.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making the game kinder to the phone battery during long sessions.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Battery-friendly games get longer sessions and better store ratings.
Terms.Example: Lowering tick rates and network polls while the app is backgrounded or idle.
Terms.CommonMistake: Keeping full update loops running on menus with no visible benefit.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Profile power draw for one combat scene and cut one always-on timer.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Shipping only the assets and binaries a specific device needs to reduce install size.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Giving each phone just the slices of the game it actually requires.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Smaller installs improve conversion and reduce uninstalls on storage-limited devices.
Terms.Example: Delivering ASTC textures for capable devices and alternate formats for others.
Terms.CommonMistake: Bundling every language and texture variant into one fat binary.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Measure install size before and after enabling device-specific asset slicing.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Handling the app when it leaves the foreground, including pause, save, and resume flows.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: What happens when the player switches away from your game and comes back.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Correct backgrounding prevents data loss, audio glitches, and network waste.
Terms.Example: Autosaving inventory and muting audio when the OS sends a pause event.
Terms.CommonMistake: Leaving network sockets and music running while the app is backgrounded.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Interrupt a match with a phone call and verify save integrity plus clean resume.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Grouping target hardware into performance classes with matching quality presets.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Sorting phones into low, mid, and high settings buckets.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Tiering lets one build serve a wide audience without overtaxing weak devices.
Terms.Example: Low tier disables shadows and caps particles while high tier enables them.
Terms.CommonMistake: Shipping one quality preset for all phones and failing on older hardware.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define three tiers with concrete feature flags and map five devices into them.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Platform rules that govern submission, privacy, monetization, and content for store approval.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The checklist stores use to accept or reject your game.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Guideline violations delay launches and can force redesigns late in production.
Terms.Example: Updating privacy disclosures and restore-purchase flows before iOS review.
Terms.CommonMistake: Ignoring guideline changes until a rejection blocks the release train.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Audit one monetization flow against current store policy and list gaps.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Remote or local messages that re-engage players when the app is not open.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Alerts that invite players back with rewards, events, or reminders.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Well-timed notifications boost retention, but spam drives uninstalls.
Terms.Example: A daily reward reminder arrives at the player's usual play window.
Terms.CommonMistake: Sending frequent generic pushes with no personalization or opt-out clarity.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Design three notification types with frequency caps and an opt-out path.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A content delivery system that loads assets by address from local or remote catalogs.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Ask for content by name and let the system fetch it from disk or the cloud.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Addressables enable smaller installs, hot updates, and controlled memory loading.
Terms.Example: Seasonal skins download on demand instead of shipping in the base package.
Terms.CommonMistake: Hardcoding bundle paths that break when catalogs are updated.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Mark one remote group addressable and load it asynchronously in a test scene.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Checking that recent changes did not break existing features.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Re-test old features after new work to make sure nothing got worse.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Regression coverage protects live quality as teams ship frequent updates.
Terms.Example: Re-run login, inventory, and combat flows after a patch changes save data.
Terms.CommonMistake: Only testing the ticket that changed and skipping adjacent critical paths.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add three regression cases for the last patch and run them on the next build.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A quick pass over critical paths to confirm a build is basically functional.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A fast sanity check before deeper testing begins.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Smoke tests catch catastrophic issues early and save QA time.
Terms.Example: Launch the build, start a match, complete a purchase flow, and exit cleanly.
Terms.CommonMistake: Calling a multi-hour exploratory pass a smoke test and delaying feedback.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write a ten-minute smoke checklist covering boot, save, combat, and quit.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Pushing a system beyond normal load to find breaking points and stability issues.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Hammer the game harder than players normally would to see what fails.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Stress testing reveals crashes, memory leaks, and server limits before launch.
Terms.Example: Spawn thousands of projectiles and AI units to measure frame time collapse.
Terms.CommonMistake: Stopping at the first failure instead of documenting the load threshold.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Increase concurrent AI agents until FPS drops below 20 and record the count.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Observing real players use a build to evaluate fun, clarity, and usability.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Watch people play and learn what confuses, frustrates, or delights them.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Playtesting surfaces design issues that automated tests and internal reviews miss.
Terms.Example: Five testers fail to find the objective until the tutorial arrow is added.
Terms.CommonMistake: Interrupting testers with coaching instead of watching natural behavior.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Run a silent 20-minute playtest and capture three friction moments with timestamps.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Automated tests that verify a small unit of code in isolation.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Tiny checks that prove one function or class behaves correctly.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Unit tests catch logic bugs early and make refactoring safer.
Terms.Example: A damage calculator test asserts critical hits multiply correctly.
Terms.CommonMistake: Writing tests that depend on full scene setup and fail for unrelated reasons.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add three unit tests around one pure gameplay function and run them in CI.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Tests that verify multiple systems work correctly together across boundaries.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Checking that connected pieces cooperate, not just each piece alone.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Integration tests catch interface mismatches that unit tests miss.
Terms.Example: A test starts a match, awards loot, and confirms inventory and analytics both update.
Terms.CommonMistake: Treating flaky end-to-end flows as unit tests and ignoring root causes.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write one integration test covering save write plus reload for inventory.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Running a build under realistic load for a long duration to find slow leaks and drift.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Leave the game running for hours to catch problems that short tests miss.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Soak tests reveal memory growth, thermal decay, and rare timing bugs.
Terms.Example: An overnight idle lobby run shows steadily rising native memory.
Terms.CommonMistake: Only soak on developer machines that never match shipping hardware.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Run a two-hour automated combat loop and chart memory every five minutes.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Validating the game across target devices, OS versions, and hardware configurations.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making sure the game works on the phones and platforms you claim to support.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Compatibility gaps cause one-star reviews and support spikes after launch.
Terms.Example: Testing login and graphics quality presets on low, mid, and high Android tiers.
Terms.CommonMistake: Testing only the newest flagship devices used by the development team.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Build a device matrix of five targets and execute the smoke suite on each.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Reviewing, prioritizing, and assigning defects based on severity and impact.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Sorting bugs so the worst problems get fixed first.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Good triage protects schedules and focuses engineering on player-facing risk.
Terms.Example: A crash on boot is marked blocker while a rare VFX pop is deferred.
Terms.CommonMistake: Prioritizing by who filed the bug instead of player impact and frequency.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Triage ten open bugs into severity buckets with owners and target milestones.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A document describing scope, environments, cases, and exit criteria for testing.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The written plan for what will be tested, how, and when it is done enough.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Plans align QA, design, and engineering on risk coverage before a milestone.
Terms.Example: A soft-launch plan covers onboarding, IAP, crash rate, and retention dashboards.
Terms.CommonMistake: Writing a plan nobody updates, so testing drifts from current risks.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Draft a one-page plan for your next milestone with entry and exit criteria.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Confirming a new package installs, launches, and passes critical checks before wider QA.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Making sure the latest build is worth testing at all.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Verification stops broken packages from wasting the whole team's day.
Terms.Example: A BVT confirms version number, login, and a match start on a clean install.
Terms.CommonMistake: Skipping verification and discovering the build cannot boot an hour later.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Automate three BVT checks that must pass before the smoke suite starts.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A trusted baseline build or output used to detect unexpected changes.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A known-good reference you compare new results against.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Golden masters catch silent regressions in rendering, audio, or deterministic sims.
Terms.Example: Screenshot diffs fail when a lighting tweak unexpectedly darkens a tutorial room.
Terms.CommonMistake: Updating the golden without review, which hides real regressions.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Capture a golden screenshot for one scene and fail CI on pixel-diff thresholds.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Comparing two or more variants with live players to measure which performs better.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Show different versions to different players and keep the winner.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A/B tests replace opinion wars with evidence for design and monetization changes.
Terms.Example: Half of new users see a shorter tutorial; retention and completion are compared.
Terms.CommonMistake: Calling a change validated after too small a sample or too short a window.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define a primary metric and minimum sample size before launching one experiment.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Testing translated text, layouts, fonts, and cultural fit across supported languages.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Checking that other languages look correct and still make sense in context.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Loc QA prevents truncated UI, broken fonts, and embarrassing mistranslations.
Terms.Example: German strings overflow a button and require layout fixes before certification.
Terms.CommonMistake: Reviewing spreadsheets only and never verifying strings in the running build.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Play one tutorial flow in a long-string language and log every overflow.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Automated continuous integration and delivery that builds, tests, and packages changes.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A robot that builds your game and runs checks every time code lands.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Pipelines shorten feedback loops and reduce human error in release packaging.
Terms.Example: Every merge triggers unit tests, a player build, and artifact upload.
Terms.CommonMistake: Allowing red pipelines to linger so broken main becomes normal.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Add one failing-gate test to CI and confirm merges are blocked until it passes.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Daily Active Users: unique players who engage with a game on a given day.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How many different people played today.
Terms.WhyItMatters: DAU helps teams track short-term engagement and the impact of updates or events.
Terms.Example: An event boosts DAU from 120,000 to 180,000 on launch day.
Terms.CommonMistake: Celebrating DAU spikes from bots or duplicated accounts as real growth.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Chart DAU for two weeks around an event and annotate content changes.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Monthly Active Users: unique players who engage within a rolling month.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How many different people played at least once this month.
Terms.WhyItMatters: MAU shows broader audience health beyond day-to-day volatility.
Terms.Example: A seasonal campaign lifts MAU even when daily numbers fluctuate.
Terms.CommonMistake: Comparing MAU across unequal month lengths without normalization.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compute DAU/MAU stickiness for the last three months and explain the trend.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Lifetime Value: estimated revenue or value a player generates over their relationship with a game.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How much a player is worth across their entire time with the game.
Terms.WhyItMatters: LTV guides acquisition spend, pricing, and retention investment.
Terms.Example: If average LTV is $12, paid campaigns must stay below that to remain profitable.
Terms.CommonMistake: Optimizing only day-one revenue while ignoring long-tail LTV.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Estimate 90-day LTV for one cohort and compare it to current CPI.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The rate at which players return to a game after their first session.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How many people come back tomorrow, next week, or next month.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Retention shows whether onboarding, content, and updates keep players engaged.
Terms.Example: Day-7 retention rises after improving the first-hour tutorial and daily rewards.
Terms.CommonMistake: Looking only at install counts while retention quietly collapses.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Report D1, D7, and D30 retention for your latest build cohort.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Average Revenue Per User across the active audience in a period.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How much revenue you earn on average from each player.
Terms.WhyItMatters: ARPU helps compare monetization strength across builds and markets.
Terms.Example: A battle pass season lifts ARPU even when DAU stays flat.
Terms.CommonMistake: Raising prices without watching conversion drop enough to hurt total revenue.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Calculate ARPU before and after a monetization change for the same cohort window.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Average Revenue Per Daily Active User for a given day.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How much money each daily player is worth on that day.
Terms.WhyItMatters: ARPDAU is a sensitive daily pulse for live ops and monetization experiments.
Terms.Example: A weekend event doubles ARPDAU while DAU rises only modestly.
Terms.CommonMistake: Judging a feature by ARPDAU alone without checking retention side effects.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Plot ARPDAU for fourteen days and mark each live ops intervention.
Synonyms: average revenue per daily active user

Terms.ShortDefinition: The rate at which players stop returning within a defined inactivity window.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How quickly players leave and do not come back.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Churn diagnosis points teams to broken onboarding, difficulty spikes, or stale content.
Terms.Example: Players who skip seven days are marked churned for reactivation campaigns.
Terms.CommonMistake: Defining churn so loosely that seasonal players look permanently lost.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Identify the top three screens last seen by churned D7 players.

Terms.ShortDefinition: How long a typical play session lasts from start to finish.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How many minutes players stick around in one sitting.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Session length informs content chunking, ad placement, and mobile comfort.
Terms.Example: A mobile puzzler targets five-minute sessions that fit a commute.
Terms.CommonMistake: Forcing long sessions with energy walls that frustrate short-session players.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Measure median session length before and after changing level length.

Terms.ShortDefinition: The percentage of players who complete a desired action such as purchase or tutorial finish.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How many people who saw an opportunity actually took it.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Conversion rates reveal friction in funnels from install to paying or completing goals.
Terms.Example: Store checkout conversion rises after simplifying the purchase confirmation screen.
Terms.CommonMistake: Optimizing conversion with dark patterns that damage long-term trust.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Map one funnel from store impression to purchase and compute step conversion.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Grouping players by shared start attributes and comparing their behavior over time.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Track players who started together and see how their journeys differ.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Cohorts expose whether changes help new players or only existing whales.
Terms.Example: Players who joined during a Halloween event retain differently than organic January installs.
Terms.CommonMistake: Averaging all users together and hiding cohort-specific regressions.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare D7 retention for two install-week cohorts around a tutorial change.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Measuring drop-off across ordered steps toward a goal.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Finding where players abandon a path you wanted them to complete.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Funnels turn vague retention problems into specific broken steps.
Terms.Example: Sixty percent of players leave between weapon pickup and first enemy kill.
Terms.CommonMistake: Tracking funnels without timestamps, so sequence errors are invisible.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Instrument a four-step tutorial funnel and prioritize the largest drop-off.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A real-money transaction inside a game for currency, items, or unlocks.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Players pay inside the app for something beyond the free download.
Terms.WhyItMatters: IAP design must balance revenue with fairness and platform compliance.
Terms.Example: A starter pack offers currency and a cosmetic at a first-purchase discount.
Terms.CommonMistake: Gatekeeping core progression behind purchases in ways that violate store rules or trust.
Terms.PracticePrompt: List every IAP and mark which are cosmetic versus power-affecting.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A time-limited progression track that rewards play, often with a premium paid track.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A seasonal checklist of rewards you unlock by playing during the season.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Battle passes monetize engagement while giving free players a clear goal ladder.
Terms.Example: A ten-week pass grants cosmetics on free and premium tracks as XP accumulates.
Terms.CommonMistake: Requiring impossible grind so premium buyers still cannot finish without more spend.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Sketch a twenty-tier pass with earn rates that a median player can complete.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Paid or organic efforts to attract new players into the game.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How you find and bring in new players.
Terms.WhyItMatters: UA efficiency determines whether growth is sustainable against LTV.
Terms.Example: A creative test lowers cost per install while preserving D7 retention.
Terms.CommonMistake: Scaling spend into channels with good installs but terrible retention.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Compare CPI and D7 retention across two creative variants for one channel.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A viral coefficient estimating how many new players each existing player brings in.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: How strongly your players recruit other players.
Terms.WhyItMatters: K-factor helps teams understand organic growth beyond paid acquisition.
Terms.Example: Invite rewards produce 0.3 new installs per active player in a season.
Terms.CommonMistake: Counting installs that would have happened anyway as viral successes.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Instrument invite sends and resulting installs, then compute a weekly K-factor.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Minimum Viable Product: the smallest version that proves core value to players.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The leanest playable version that tests whether the idea works.
Terms.WhyItMatters: An MVP reduces wasted production by validating fun and market fit early.
Terms.Example: Ship one dungeon loop with basic progression before building the full world map.
Terms.CommonMistake: Calling a feature-complete product an MVP and delaying learning for months.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Define an MVP feature list that can be playtested in four weeks or less.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Releasing a game in limited regions or audiences to gather data before global launch.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: A practice launch in a smaller market before going worldwide.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Soft launches reveal retention, monetization, and stability issues with lower risk.
Terms.Example: Launch in two countries, tune onboarding for two weeks, then expand globally.
Terms.CommonMistake: Treating soft launch as a tiny marketing push with no instrumentation or tuning time.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Write soft-launch success criteria for retention, crash rate, and ARPDAU.

Terms.ShortDefinition: Ongoing updates, events, and content that keep a shipped game active and healthy.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: Running the game after launch with events, fixes, and fresh content.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Live ops sustains engagement and revenue long after initial release.
Terms.Example: Weekly events, seasonal passes, and balance patches across the first year.
Terms.CommonMistake: Shipping calendars so dense that content quality and QA collapse.
Terms.PracticePrompt: Plan a four-week live ops calendar with owners, goals, and rollback plans.

Terms.ShortDefinition: When a project's feature list grows beyond the original plan without matching time or budget.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The game keeps gaining new ideas faster than the team can build them.
Terms.WhyItMatters: Scope creep delays launches, burns teams out, and dilutes the core experience.
Terms.Example: A small puzzle game adds multiplayer, crafting, and a battle pass before the first release.
Terms.CommonMistake: Accepting every stakeholder request without cutting something else.
Terms.PracticePrompt: List five proposed features and cut two that do not serve the MVP core loop.

Terms.ShortDefinition: A living reference that captures vision, systems, constraints, and content goals.
Terms.SimpleExplanation: The shared write-up of what the game is and how its systems should work.
Terms.WhyItMatters: A clear GDD reduces misalignment across design, art, engineering, and production.
Terms.Example: Pillars, core loop, camera rules, and progression charts live in one editable doc.
